title: The boy who told the truth
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hook: a boy at a teacher's door who can't name his father's family
carry: the plain truth, satya, opened the teacher's door
tomorrow: why would a law book call itself 'remembered'?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Manusmriti, read whole: go back for the page. Now a new stretch, on what the tradition has kept and what it has let go, and it opens at a door.

Forms always want it: father's name, family, where you're from. A boy in the Chandogya Upanishad is about to be asked, and he can't answer. He asked his mother first. Her answer, in paraphrase: I don't know your father's family. When I was young I moved about a great deal, serving others, and that's when you came. I am Jabala, you are Satyakama; call yourself Satyakama Jabala. So now he stands before a teacher, Gautama, who asks the question every form asks. What's your family? And the boy opens his mouth.
screen: `FATHER'S NAME, FAMILY.` → `HIS MOTHER DOESN'T KNOW.` → `AT THE TEACHER'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: He tells him exactly what his mother said. No polish, no borrowed father. I don't know my family, sir. My mother was young and moved about, serving, and she doesn't know either. I am Satyakama Jabala. Then the teacher answers, and that's the turn of the story. In paraphrase: no one but a brahmin could speak like that. Bring firewood, my dear; I'll take you as a student. You have not left the truth. Readers hear that line two ways. Some say the teacher read the boy's birth from his honesty. Others hear the truth itself deciding: whoever speaks like that is a brahmin, whatever the family. Either way, a teacher takes on a student who can name no father's family, because of one plain truth. His name says it: Satyakama, one who loves the truth. This is satya, truthfulness, one of the oldest Hindu virtues, and here it does something remarkable: it opens a door that birth alone would have kept shut. The tradition kept this story and still tells it, and many teachers set it beside the law books' rules of birth to ask which one to live by. For us it starts somewhere plain: when you don't know, in a temple, a classroom or a family argument, the Hindu answer begins with saying so.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW MY FAMILY.` · `YOU HAVE NOT LEFT THE TRUTH.` · `TWO WAYS TO HEAR IT.` · then, large: `SATYA OPENED THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for a minute, the way the boy walked up to the teacher's door: one step, one breath. If walking isn't possible right now, rest your hands open on your knees and feel each breath arrive. Then sit, and let the rest of the bell be quiet.
Kept and rejected: what the tradition holds on to, and what it lets go. Satyakama's story, and its satya, is one it kept.
For the road: the plain truth, satya, opened the teacher's door. A boy with no family name to give proved it. See you tomorrow.
